input.vignette:
A 4-month-old male infant is evaluated during a routine well-child check. The parents report difficulty weaning him from nighttime feedings, noting that he becomes extremely distressed after 3-4 hours without feeding and is only consoled by being fed.

Growth assessment reveals a decline from the 25th to the 5th percentile in length, while weight remains at the 25th percentile. Physical examination reveals distinctive facial fullness, significantly distended abdomen, and thin limbs. The liver edge extends to the iliac crest, but the spleen is not enlarged.

A blood sample demonstrates a characteristic milky white layer on its surface.

Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

Options:
A. Prader-Willi syndrome
B. Congenital hyperinsulinism
C. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
E. Gaucher disease
F. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
G. Glycogen storage disease type 1
H. Tay-Sachs disease
I. Familial hypercholesterolemia
J. Niemann-Pick disease type A

knowledge_chunks.title: Pediatrics_Nelson
knowledge_chunks.text: Fetuses subjected to abnormal maternal, placental, or fetal conditions that restrain growth are a high-risk group and traditionally classified as having intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).The terms IUGR and SGA (small for gestational age) are notsynonymous. IUGR represents a deviation from expectedgrowth patterns. The decreased fetal growth associated with IUGR is an adaptation to unfavorable intrauterine conditions that result in permanent alterations in metabolism, growth, anddevelopment. IUGR most frequently occurs with a variety ofmaternal conditions that are associated with preterm delivery.SGA describes an infant whose birth weight is statistically lessthan the 10th percentile or two standard deviations below themean birth weight for gestational age. The cause of SGA may bepathologic, as in an infant with IUGR, or nonpathologic, as in an infant who is small but otherwise healthy (Table 60-1).
